scenes.text: Here's the same burner gas, burning two ways. With the air hole open, the flame is blue and hard to see. Close the air hole, and you get a tall yellow flame. Now hold a cold white dish over each one for a few seconds. Over the blue flame, the dish just mists up with a little water. Over the yellow flame, its underside turns black. That black is soot, which is carbon. Same fuel, different products. So what changed?

Burning has a chemistry name, combustion. It's a reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases energy as heat and light. Burner gas is natural gas, which is mostly methane, C H four, a hydrocarbon, made of only carbon and hydrogen. Here's the key to predicting the products. When a hydrocarbon burns, its carbon takes oxygen from the air, as much as the supply allows, and its hydrogen becomes water, an oxide of hydrogen.

When there's plenty of oxygen, every carbon atom gets two oxygen atoms, and becomes carbon dioxide. Every pair of hydrogen atoms gets one oxygen atom, and becomes water. That's complete combustion, and it's what the blue flame is doing. You can test the products. The mist on the cold dish is water, and the gas turns limewater milky, so it's carbon dioxide.

To balance it, do carbon first, then hydrogen, and leave oxygen until last. Oxygen gas is an element on its own, so changing its number doesn't upset anything else. One carbon gives one carbon dioxide. Four hydrogens give two waters. Now count the oxygen on the right: two in carbon dioxide, and two in the waters, makes four. That's two oxygen molecules. And because water leaves a flame as steam, it's written as a gas.

Quick prediction. Butane, C four H ten, the gas in camping stoves. Carbon gives four carbon dioxides, and hydrogen gives five waters. That's thirteen oxygen atoms on the right. How many oxygen molecules is that?

Six and a half, because thirteen oxygen atoms make six and a half pairs. But half a molecule can't react, so double everything. Two butane plus thirteen oxygen gives eight carbon dioxide plus ten water. Check: eight carbon, twenty hydrogen and twenty-six oxygen on each side.

Now close the air hole. Less air mixes with the gas, so there isn't enough oxygen to give every carbon atom two. Some carbon atoms get only one, and become carbon monoxide, C O. Some get none at all, and stay as tiny specks of carbon, which is soot. Those hot specks glow, and that's what makes the flame yellow. Burning without enough oxygen is called incomplete combustion. The hydrogen still ends up as water.

The equations follow the same counting. With some oxygen missing, two methane plus three oxygen gives two carbon monoxide plus four water. With even less, methane plus one oxygen gives soot plus two water. The less oxygen there is for each methane, the further down the ladder the carbon goes. So here's the way to remember it. Plenty of oxygen, carbon takes two. Less oxygen, it takes one. Least, it takes none.

This matters. Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas with no colour and no smell, so you can't tell it's there. Soot dirties surfaces, and incomplete burning wastes energy too. That's why gas heaters need good ventilation, and homes use carbon monoxide alarms. In the lab, combustion is done with your teacher supervising, safety glasses on, long hair tied back, in a well-ventilated room, and the Bunsen goes back to the yellow safety flame whenever you're not heating.

The fuel matters too. A metal has no carbon and no hydrogen, so when magnesium burns in oxygen, the only product is the metal oxide. No carbon dioxide, and no water. Magnesium burns with a brilliant white light, so bright you shouldn't look straight at it, and leaves white magnesium oxide. Charges fix the formula: plus two and minus two, so it's M g O, not M g O two.

Copper doesn't burst into flame. Heat copper foil in a Bunsen flame, and its surface slowly turns black, as a coating of copper oxide forms. Copper is plus two here, so the oxide is C u O, and two copper plus oxygen gives two copper oxide. Magnesium flares, copper only darkens. That difference in vigour is a clue to how reactive each metal is, and you'll use it to rank metals.
Your turn. Pentane, C five H twelve, is part of petrol. Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of pentane vapour, including states. Pause here to answer.

Five carbons give five carbon dioxides. Twelve hydrogens give six waters. That's ten plus six, sixteen oxygen atoms, so eight oxygen molecules. C five H twelve plus eight O two gives five C O two plus six H two O, all gases. Writing sixteen O two counts atoms, not molecules.
Last one. A gas heater in a poorly ventilated room burns propane, C three H eight, making only carbon monoxide and water. Write the balanced equation. Pause here to answer.

Three carbons give three carbon monoxides, and eight hydrogens give four waters. That's seven oxygen atoms, three and a half O two, so double. Two propane plus seven oxygen gives six carbon monoxide plus eight water. Writing carbon dioxide is the classic slip. The oxygen ran short, so carbon takes only one.

So when a hydrocarbon burns, its hydrogen becomes water, and the oxygen supply decides how far the carbon gets. Metals burn to metal oxides, like this magnesium oxide. Drop it into dilute hydrochloric acid, and it dissolves, with no fizzing. Put marble chips, calcium carbonate, into the same acid, and they fizz. Both use up the acid, but they can't be making the same products. How can we predict acid-base and acid-carbonate products?
